page.title: Mayhem Encyclopedia Custom Articles
page.t:
You begin your journey in the outer border galaxies - regions shaped by two great conflicts that defined the modern era.

Centuries ago, the Terraformers were corrupted when terraformer scientist Martin Winters altered its termination protocols. The machines abandoned their mandate to build worlds and began exterminating biological life. The resulting First Terraformer Conflict saw the Terrans fight for survival against their own creations - the machines now known as the Xenon.

In the centuries that followed, tensions between the Terrans and the Commonwealth races escalated into a series of wars. After five major conflicts, the Commonwealth - Argon, Boron, Paranid, Split, and Teladi - were expelled from the Terran core systems and permitted to settle only in the frontier sectors. These outer regions were placed under the authority of Terracorp, a powerful Terran corporation tasked with managing what were termed "external affairs."

The border galaxies remain unstable. Xenon forces persist in significant numbers, internal rivalries weaken the Commonwealth factions, and the Terrans maintain only a limited expeditionary presence.

Whether you stand with the exiled factions, serve Terran interests, or arise from the machine legacy of the original catastrophe, you begin as a minor actor in a divided frontier - where power is fragile and history is written by the victors.

The following text is an excerpt from a book written by your father 16 years ago.

\033X... on my way here. The most important thing to remember is that history is never with us, the people. The bad guys always win and they tell their children what they want to hear. Obedience doesn't make men, free will does. You have to read between the lines and accept the truth without looking back on your actions. That's what this rebellion is about: understanding the world without fear, tears or laughters. Do you think that Terracorp pities us? Can you imagine them approving a plan that would make them less important in this galaxy? Or maybe you have been fed on sweet lies and illusions. Then let me refresh your memory on the past...

As you probably know from school, the Terrans started the terraforming of thousands of planets centuries ago. In their desperate attempt to control everything, they built an AI capable of doing the hard work, the Xenons, who later turned against their people. What you don't know however is that the Commonwealth tried to fight the Xenons, but instead of helping them, the Terrans declared war on them because of their mad scientists believing that some Xenons were still active and working in the interest of their ruthless empire.

After five consecutive wars, the Commonwealth was defeated. Each faction, the Argons, the Borons, the Paranids, the Splits and the Teladis were banned from the core galaxies. For many years, they hid in the dark corners of the known universe, while the Terrans were creating Terracorp, a giant company that will be used to deal with the "outside problems". From this day, everything was made private and the Terrans managed to influence the people to believe that they were unimpeachable.

Some years later, they had this idea of terraforming new planets... They didn't imagine how strong the Xenons had become over the time, and Terracorp stole billions of credits in taxes to send Terrans to their death against these vicious machines. But then, the desire for more profits made them change their minds. Instead of sending more military ships to the galaxies controlled by the Xenons, they auctioned these sectors to the remnant of the Commonwealth, making them believe that they could rise again and become the strong factions they always wanted to be. The core sectors would still be closed to them and they will always stay at the edge of the conquered universe, but they were free to exist and they wouldn't have to hide anymore. They accepted the offer and bought hundreds of galaxies infested with Xenons. Of course, this threat was hidden from them by the Terrans. What they did tell them however was that Terracorp was in charge of these outer border galaxies. Some rules were designed to limit the expansion of each faction. Obviously, this lead to internal wars, and without leaders able to reunite everyone, we stood no chance against the Terrans. We had to deal with the cupidity and the thirst for power on one side, and the Xenons on the other side...

\End of the excerpt.

Each sector has different statistics displayed in the sector description of your galaxy map or in the Ministry of War menu:

Population: the maximum amount of people any Outpost can have. Your global supply cap is determined based on population. For more information about the supply mechanic, see the Empire -> Supply section.

Research rate: the speed at which your Research stations will operate. Also has an effect on Hacking stations.

Station support: the maximum number of stations allowed. This includes all docks and factories except Pirate bases and Company stations.

Dejure owner: when the AI decides to invade a sector, it looks at various things, including the sector value, which is greatly increased when the dejure owner is the same as their faction. Dejure sectors cannot be bought, but they can be captured.

Company: if a company is assigned to a safe sector, a Trading station will appear. This station trades various wares that depends on the company.

Abnormal signals: some dangerous threats could be more interested in sectors that have a stronger signal.

Terran memory: Some Terran ships have been abandoned a long time ago when the Terrans were trying to terraform the planets. While the Terrans have returned, they had left some debris and wreckage behind that can help your Research stations study Terran technologies. Terrans are considered as the dejure owner of Terran memory sectors.

Outpost production and consumption: each Outpost produces a type of food, and consumes another one. The selection of this food depends on the sector.

The number of resources you can produce and trade has been greatly reduced to make the economy focus on the crafting part of the game. You'll notice that the price of everything has been adjusted and greatly lowered, as well as possible margins.

Because everything is now focused on crafting, every resource you see being transported is going to be used by either an Outpost to craft ships and stations, or another factory to manufacture a higher tier product.

Every ship comes from an Outpost and there is no artificial spawning. If you see a ship, that means that a faction has paid for it, with real resources.

The galaxy is divided between several competing powers.

The six major powers - Argon, Boron, Paranid, Split, Teladi, and Terran - control established territories and wage conventional wars for expansion.

Beyond them exist machine-origin factions born from the Terraformer catastrophe. The Xenon remain the primary machine threat. The OCV represent a separate and highly aggressive machine network. Phanon is a rogue terraformer intelligence whose objectives may align with or oppose the player, depending on circumstances.

Independent and irregular forces also operate throughout the frontier. The Renegades are decentralized warbands that exploit instability and overextension, while the Yaki persist as a criminal organization. For more information about the Renegades, see Mechanics -> Renegades.

Each major faction begins with defined territory and will attempt to conquer additional sectors. For more details, see Warfare -> Invasions and Warfare -> Squadrons.

If you are coming from Litcube's Universe \(LU\), note that Phanon has been reimagined as a rogue terraformer faction rather than a corporation. The OCV is a completely new machine faction and does not follow LU behavior patterns. Both Xenon and OCV forces can conquer sectors.

Vanilla missions have been replaced by a new system. There are 15 procedural missions:

Patrol \(fight\): hunt Xenon fleets in a given sector. The Xenons will appear only when your own ship or any of your fleet leaders enters the sector. Each kill will grant you some credits and reputation, but you won't receive any if you just wait for other ships to do your job.

Suppression \(fight\): factions are often at war against each other. This mission asks you to destroy existing ships of an enemy faction. The factions against whom you are in permanent war will be prioritized.

Bait \(fight\): capture a nearby abandoned miner ship to attract Kha'ak ships from deep space. Each kill will grant you some credits and reputation, and you will get the ship if you succeed in protecting it.

Defense \(fight\): the Xenons have built a Jump Beacon nearby and they are targeting a station. Protect the station and destroy the beacon.

Provision \(trade\): a station needs various wares. You can deliver them with any of your ships. The reward is always based on the average price of all wares.

Acquisition \(trade\): sometimes the AI will send his Tugs to capture abandoned ships. These ships can be used in their Outposts when needed, or sold to you through these missions.

Deliveries \(trade\): a shady character will ask you to do multiple deliveries. Make sure you can defend yourself, as the parcels you ought to deliver are valuable to some pirates.

Prospecting \(think\): some asteroids need to be scanned in a given sector. If you've already scan all existing asteroids in this sector, new ones will be created.

Collection \(think\): Artefacts have been dropped around a given sector. You must find them and bring them back to the station that gave you the mission. Artefacts come in a flying ware that the AI cannot loot.

Exploration \(think\): deploy Advanced satellites at given coordinates. An error margin of 5 km is allowed. Note that there is a command to move to coordinates in the Navigation section.

Rescue \(think\): capture an abandoned ship and get it back to its station, with all passengers alive onboard. As a reward, you can keep the ship.

Police \(think\): find a criminal and bring him to justice. As a reward, you can keep his ship.

Intel \(fight\): go to a station enemy to the mission giver and wait to scan it for data collection. You must fully stop your ship for the scan to progress. Only you, with your own ship, can complete this mission. During the scanning process, local Police can detect you and attack you.

VIP \(think\): you must transport one passenger to a nearby factory. Upon completion, the factory will receive a temporary production bonus. Docking is required to accept this mission.

Supplies \(trade\): bring some resources to a nearby factory. The products are a custom order and will not affect the station where you get the mission. However, the targeted factory will use the resources you supply. Docking is required to accept this mission.

To see the mission briefing offered by a station, you can either dock at that station, use the Mission Briefing command under the Additional Ship Commands section of the ship console, or go to Personal Console -> Personal journal. You can then and accept the offer or abandon that mission if you previously accepted it. Some missions require you to dock at a station to see the briefing. The Mission Briefing command allows you to accept a mission from any of your ships. Missions are periodically generated and do not have a time limit, but they will eventually expire if they are not taken.

Outposts are the main stations of every faction, including yours. They serve as local headquarters and also as factories with their ability to build ships, lasers, missiles and shields. They are crucial in your development, because they represent the only way you have to build stations and ships.

Outposts do not work magically. People live inside and work together to manufacture everything you need. In exchange, you must provide them with food if you do not want them to starve to death. Each Outpost produces a certain type of food and consumes another one, depending on the sector \(see the Sectors Stats section\). The consumption can be removed with the No Food Consumption perk. 

If an Outpost has fewer than 30 people, then the Outpost will attract 20 people per Outpost consumption cycle \(default: 10 minutes\). When an Outpost has at least 30 people, it attracts more people at a rate of 9 people \(default growth rate\) per cycle, though this growth rate is reduced depending on how populated the Outpost is. The Population Stability perk removes growth rate penalties, but it doubles food consumption and is mutually exclusive with No Food Consumption. Up to 5 people can be transferred between Outposts, but there is a 33% chance that at least 1 person dies during transit.

People can work on multiple projects at the same time without any penalty. 

Outposts can be affected by various events that will have unfortunate effects. The more people you have, the more chance you get of generating an event. You can restrict the maximum number of people in each of your Outpost through the Administration menu. You can avoid these events with the Insurance Policy perk. Harder difficulties reduce the effectiveness of Insurance Policy.

Only Traders and ships that run a Trade Run commands can dock to NPC Outposts. However, NPC Outposts will never sell Crystals, Hull Plating, Computer Components, Quantum Tubes, and Silicon Wafers because these wares are shipbuilding materials.

You can upgrade an Outpost to a Capital Shipyard. This costs Outposts, Blue Crystals, and Green Crystals \(cost depends on difficulty\). In exchange, a Capital Shipyard gives 10% more ship specialization, 2 additional perk slots, 1.2x recycling factor, and more capital ship docking slots.

Companies are minor factions that stand neutral in the many wars that are fought over the galaxy. They have their own Trading stations that trade different wares depending on the company, and their own Traders that can survive any hostilities between two factions. They also have mercenaries that you can hire via your Personal console.

Companies are sector-based and will only build a Trading Station when the sector is safe, ie. not Unknown and not Xenon. A sector you own is considered safe.

Destroying company assets is illegal and is punished by a heavy fine.

The general rule to expand your own empire is that you only need to unload an Outpost or a factory into an empty sector to conquer it. However, to expand into other territories, you first need to destroy all faction stations that are not owned by a company. Besides, capturing a new sector will cost you some reputation with adjacent owners \(except for the first one\). You must be very careful if you don't want to have a negative reputation with a neighbour and risk of being attacked on sight by his ships.

Through your Personal console, you can abandon a sector you already own or give it to another faction if your reputation is high enough. Giving a sector to another faction will give you a favor point unless that faction demanded that sector in an ultimatum.

On harder difficulties, factions may issue an ultimatum against you and demand control over one of your sectors. You can comply with their demand or refuse by ignoring their ultimatum after missing the 1 hour deadline, abandoning that sector, or giving that sector to another faction other than the faction who gave the ultimatum. Refusing an ultimatum will result in a war declaration.

Don't be too eager to conquer new sectors! Each of them can draw the attention of Xenons or Pirates, and you better have enough firepower to defend your existing assets before going deeper into unknown territory.

Crafting is one of the most important features of Mayhem. Ships, stations, lasers, missiles and equipment can be crafted with various resources that you can all produce by building factories in your sectors. In Mayhem, Saturn Complex Hubs and Vanilla Complexes have been deactivated, but the costs of many things have been modified to keep the game balanced.

All crafting costs are based on the average price of the product you're trying to make, divided by the number of resources it requires.

Each Outpost has its own specialization levels in different areas. The more projects you complete in a specific area \(ship, laser, missile, or station\) the better you become at it; that means that both research and time costs will be reduced. Specialization has diminishing returns.

By default, base specialization ranges from 0% to 20%. Base specialization can be further increased via terraforming effects and Terraforming Efficiency 4, a milestone perk. Specific specialization can be further increased via the Cheaper Stations perk, Renegade plot completion, and the Capital Shipyard. The AI has dynamic specialization.

Cancelling a project will always give you back the resources you've invested.

Crafting a ship requires people.

All ships come with a default set of shields and lasers. Laser crafting is optional but opens up custom loadouts.

Workers are automated ships that are used to run your empire and make your life easier. Each Outpost and some of your factories have a limited number of slots to which you can assign different types of Workers. You can see these limitations, and other options, in the Administration tab of your Outposts.

Agents: they operate either an Outpost or a factory. If working for an Outpost, they will look for a job from the jobs list you define in the Logistics menu of the Outpost manager. If affected to a factory, they will look to import resources and export products to any of your other stations. Unlike Traders, Agents never trade with stations that you do not own. Agents are synchronized with each other and also with Traders.

Explorers: their only goal is to ensure that every reachable sector is monitored by an Advanced Satellite. If they cannot find one from your stations, they will wait until it becomes available. They do not purchase Satellites from other factions. Unlike other Workers, Explorers operate with a fixed range of 15 sectors and ignore the "Max. sector distance for all Workers" setting.

Looters: they look for abandoned wares in all reachable sectors and bring them back to their homebase.

Miners: when affected to an Outpost or a Quantum Tube Fab, they will mine the debris in the sector and unload their cargo to their homebase when full. Mobile mining fleets no longer exist. In Mayhem, only Ore and Silicon Wafers can be mined, as well as colored crystals and minerals that can be sold or used to craft equipment through your Outposts' hangars.

Traders: ST and UT don't exist any more. Traders are the only Workers that can interact with factories you don't own. Other factions can send their own Traders to your Outposts if you allow them to. All Traders and Agents are synchronized with each other: they "lock" the ware in the station they're heading to, thus avoiding multiple Traders going to the same place for the same ware.

Tugs: they look for abandoned ships in all reachable sectors and bring them back to their homebase. Some mission ships or other special ships, such as the ones that emit a remnant signal, cannot be captured by Tugs.

The AI uses the exact same Workers as you, powered by the same scripts. The AI, however, has an additional Worker: the Service ships, that are only here to give some flavor to the game, without any particular effect.

All Workers respect the 'Max. sector distance' range setting of their homebase. For performance reasons, Agents and Traders will not go above 8 sectors. This is configurable in the config files.

There are two main screens that will help you to manage your logistics: the Agents menu and the Traders menu. Both are found in the Logistics tab of the Outpost manager. It's important to note that Agents only manage your own stations. If you want to interact with the stations of other factions, you'll need a Trader. The wares that Traders are allowed to exchange from and to your Outposts must be manually added to the Traders list. Each of your factories has import-export thresholds that you can set in their Station parameters menu. Agents and Traders will always check these thresholds: a first time before going there, and a second time on arrival \(export only\). Each Outpost and each factory can be configured to accept or forbid either your Traders or NPC Traders. When you build your first Outpost, it can be wise to allow other Traders to dock in order to buy the things you need from them, especially food.

When an AI Trader comes to one of your stations, he can buy products or sell resources. If the station doesn't have enough money to buy all wares from a Trader, you will be notified \(your main account will NOT be debited\). Note that the AI will not trade at any price; its tolerance to unfair price is based on your trade rank. Fortunately there is an Automatic Pricing setting in all your factories. It is recommended to leave it on.

All Traders are synchronized and "lock" the station they're heading to, thus avoiding multiple Traders going to the same place for the same ware.

Each station has a very important setting: "Max. sector distance for all Workers". This defines the range at which your Agents and Traders will look for trading partners, but not only, because all your Workers are affected by this value, including Explorers. Note that the "Reachable factories" job setting depends on that parameter as well.

Station parameters can be modified either through the vanilla menu or the new Station settings menu in your Personal console. Note that only through the latter is it possible to setup an automatic transfer of credits.

Due to its flexibility and the full control you can have over your Agents, Logistics is properly one of the most complex aspects of Mayhem. In this section, we will see how to setup a logistics in order to produce the required materials for station crafting, which are Teladianium, Raster Oil and Ore. You will need the following:

- A sector with a minimum of 8 support.
- 4 TS used as Agents. They can be slow and cheap, as they don't need to leave the sector.
- An Outpost to produce the ships and craft the stations you need.

Right from the beginning, when you unload your first Outpost from your TL, you have enough resources to build all the stations you need:

- Chelt Space Aquarium: produces Chelts Meat out of Energy Cells.
- Chemical Lab: produces Chemicals out of Waste. Waste is automatically produced in Outposts.
- Food Preparation Facility: produces C-Ration out of Protein Paste.
- Ore Mine: produces Ore out of C-Ration. You can also harvest Ore and Silicon Wafers with Miners from your Outpost.
- Protein Paste Blending Facility: produces Protein Paste out of Waste.
- Rastar Refinery: produces Rastar Oil out of Chelts Meat.
- Teladianium Foundry: produces Teladianium out of Chemicals.

Once you have all your stations, head to your Logistics screen and add the following:

- Import Teladianium from local factories. The most expensive factory costs around 4,500 Teladianium.
- Import Ore from local factories. The most expensive factory costs around 7,500 Ore.
- Export Energy Cells to local factories. We assume you have the Solar panels perk. If not, you can either buy Energy Cells from outside with a Trader, or make a Solar Power Plant if you have enough support in your sector.
- Export Waste to local factories.

One approach is to assign 1 Agent to each of the following stations: Outpost, Food Preparation Facility, Rastar Refinery and Teladianium Foundry. Remember that Agents assigned to a factory take care of both importing and exporting. For instance, in your Food Preparation Facility, your Agent will import Protein Paste from your local producer, and export C-Ration to the local mine. Another example: your Agent in your Rastar Refinery will import Chelts Meat, and export the Rastar Oil to your Outpost because no factories need it.

A second and better approach is to assign some Agents to your Outpost. A good rule of thumb is that 1 Agent can handle 2-3 factories. Go back to the Logistics screen add the following:

- Import Chemicals from local factories.
- Import Chelt Meat from local factories. 
- Import Protein Paste from local factories. 
- Import C-Ration from local factories.
- Export Chemicals to local factories.
- Export Chelt Meat to local factories.
- Export C-Ration to local factories.
- Export Protein Paste to local factories.

If set up correctly, your Agents will export all the basic and intermediate resources; they will also import the final products back to the Outpost. With the second approach, your agents will import and export between your Outpost and each of the factories. This centralizes Outpost logistics within its sector.

If you still have room in your sector, consider building an Advanced Satellite Factory. They can be used to make an Explorer, and you can sell the satellites for a good price quite easily. Plus, Advanced Satellites are easy to manufacture, as they require only Energy Cells.

If you need more materials but don't have any more free station slots in your sector, you can use an ST-cargo ship equipped with a Mobile Factory Kit \(craftable from the Hangar -> Upgrade Ships menu of your Outposts\). However, it is less efficient than normal factories.

The easiest way to acquire ships, other than capturing or buying them through a trade mission, is to craft them with resources. However, to craft a ship, you must unlock its blueprint. Blueprints are listed in all Research stations and in the Blueprints menu of your Personal console. There are four ways to gain research towards a blueprint.

The first way is to scan a ship. Scanning data requires a Data Scanner that you own from game start \(inventory item\) and the assignment of its associated hotkey. Scanning a ship is free and safe, but can be very tedious, as it unlocks only a small part of the Blueprint, and bigger ships require multiple scans of several ships of the same type to be fully unlocked.

The second and much faster way to unlock blueprints is with Research stations. These stations allow you to study any ship in order to unlock their blueprints to all your Outposts. Each sector has a different research rate, so make sure to build them in the best sectors. Note that each project can be interrupted and resumed at any time. Research stations do not depend on people. Terran ships can be researched only in sectors that have Terran memory \(see your Galaxy map\).

The third way is to successfully board a ship. The first time you successfully board a ship will grant you up to the first 25% of its blueprint.

The fourth way is to recycle a ship. In most cases, you gain different amounts of a ship's blueprint depending on how much you know about its blueprint. You get 40% research if you have 0-25% research completed, 25% if you have 26-50% completed, and 10% if you have 51-85% completed. The maximum amount of research you can get from recycling is 85%. The remaining 15% must be completed either via the Data Scanner or Research Stations. 

There are three exceptions to recycling. First, for advanced ships, only the first 50% of their blueprints can be unlocked via recycling. Second, OCV ships cannot be recycled if their blueprints are unlocked or if their blueprints have 85% or more research unlocked. Third, joining the OCV locks you out of research, but you get guaranteed blueprints in exchange.

Supply determines how many ships your empire can support. You start with a base amount of supply determined by difficulty.

A sector must have an Outpost in order to generate supply. Each Outpost provides supply equal to 5 times its maximum population. 

Your total supply is equal to your starting supply plus the supply generated by your Outposts. You can increase your total supply by expanding into additional sectors or by terraforming planets, which raises local population.

Every ship you own consumes supply. In general, larger and more powerful ships require more supply than smaller ones. Xenon ships consume 25% less supply, while OCV ships consume 50% more. Stations and infrastructure do not consume supply; only ships contribute to supply usage.

If your fleet's total supply usage exceeds your available supply, ship construction and maintenance costs will increase proportionally to how far you exceed the limit. Additionally, other factions will respond to your overextension. You can reduce supply usage by retiring or losing ships, either through recycling or destruction.

Difficulty also affects total supply:
- Easy: 6x
- Normal: 3x
- Hard: 2x
- Insane: 1x

In your Personal console, you'll see a Maintenance menu. It's very important that you keep an eye on this, because ship maintenance can easily get out of control. Each ship has a maintenance cost that increases over time if the ship remains undocked, depending on its maintenance factor. That means that your ships are getting old and at some point, you might want to consider sending them for a ship inspection in order to reset their maintenance factor to 100%.

The maintenance factor will not increase if the ship is equipped with a Mobile Maintenance Kit. A ship docked at an Outpost with the Dry dock perk will incur reduced maintenance costs.

With the exception of Phanon ships \(requires main plot completion\), Private Corp. ships, and Yaki ships \(if you have infamy\), all ships not made by your origin faction cost 35% more maintenance. Supply also affects maintenance costs: if your empire uses up more supply than it can support, then all your ships will cost more maintenance. For more information about the supply mechanic, see the Supply section.

On harder difficulties, sectors and Jump Beacons cost maintenance. Insane difficulty increases all maintenance costs by 50%.

Workers automatically get repaired and maintained. Fleet followers have special settings that you can adjust regarding auto-repair and auto-maintenance.

Boarding is largely the same as vanilla boarding. To begin a boarding operation, you need marines, boarding pods, and a ship that can fire boarding pods. Most M6, M8, and capital ships can fire boarding pods.

Pirate bases are essential for early boarding operations. They sell boarding pods and more skilled marines.

Your Outpost can provide the necessities to conduct more boarding operations. Boarding pods can be crafted at your Outpost. Marines can be recruited from your Outpost, but they start with low skill levels - just enough to board an M6 or TM as long as they have 2 marines with enough hacking skill supporting them at the hacking stage. You can increase their initial fighting stat by having the Pirate contract perk unlocked at your outpost. Alternatively, allying with the Xenon during the main plot will give you improved recruits. Recruiting marines at your Outpost requires your Outpost to have at least 75% of its population.

Boarding ships comes with reputation costs, and the act of boarding may earn you infamy.

Unlike vanilla, ships have more internal defenses. All M6 and TM-class ships do not have internal defenses, with the exception of mercenary ships which have all three types of defenses. However, capital ships have a chance to spawn with defenses. On Insane difficulty, the chances are doubled. Xenon and OCV ships are guaranteed to contain defenses.

After a successful boarding operation, the enemy team makes one last stand. This stage is independent of your marines' fighting skill and depends only on how many marines survived after hacking the core. The more marines you have on the ship after hacking the core, the more additional losses you will incur.

If the boarded ship had a bounty or was a Renegade roamer, you get rewards as if you had destroyed the ship. Boarding a Renegade roamer gives you more crystals than if you had destroyed it. If it had any followers upon capture, you can issue the boarded ship any attack command. This will cause all its followers to turn to your control.

This page summarizes global ship mechanics, faction traits, and sector effects. These rules apply universally unless otherwise stated.

Global Ship Rules
- Xenon and OCV ignore Xenon, OCV, and Phanon ships.
- Xenon, OCV, and Phanon ships have significantly reduced crew costs.
- Xenon-aligned players pay no upkeep costs for any ships.
- Foreign ships cost +35% maintenance, excluding Private Corp. and OWPs. Phanon ships are excluded from this penalty after the main plot.


Ship Traits

1. Commonwealth Races
- Boron ships: +10% hull regeneration every 30 minutes, but generally lower speed.
- Split ships: +20% crew cost, -3% material cost.
- Paranid ships: -20% crew cost, +3% material cost.
- Teladi ships: Weaker shields but heavier hull plating.
- Yaki ships:
 a. With infamy: -50% crew cost and exemption from the foreign maintenance penalty.
 b. Without infamy: +100% crew cost.

2. Special Factions
- Xenon ships:
 a. -50% Hull Plating
 b. -50% Computer Components
 c. -25% Supply
 d. +100% Quantum Tubes
- OCV ships:
 a. -50% Hull Plating
 b. -50% Quantum Tubes
 c. +100% Computer Components
 d. +50% Supply
- Kha'ak ships:
 a. +5% hull regeneration every 30 minutes.
 b. Can collect any cargo, including Plasma Beam Cannons.
 c. Normally obtainable only through capture. Studying recycled Kha'ak ships may reveal their secrets.

3. Sector Effects (OCV)
- Abnormal signal strength reduces ship costs for ships built in the sector.
- High signal strength accelerates OCV takeover.
- Sectors without abnormal signals cannot build OCV ships.

4. Ship Equipment
- All ships come pre-equipped based on class:
 - Capital ships (M1, M2, M7, TL): Docking Computer, Triplex Scanner
 - M1 and Dockable M2, M7: Transporter Device, Carrier Repair Module
 - M6, M8, TM: Docking Computer
 - M8: CCDS MK1-MK3, Triplex Scanner
 - TM: Boost Extension, Transporter Device, Carrier Repair Module

The galaxy is dynamic, and so are faction relations. The rules are as follows:

1. Factions are "Neutral" when no invasion is in progress between them, or when they have signed a Truce. A Truce may be signed after a sector conquest if no further invasions are active. Truces are temporary.

2. Factions are "Friend" when bound by an Unbreakable Alliance or a Coalition.

3. Factions are "Foe" when an invasion is in progress, during a Total War, or when a Permanent War exists with the player.

4. On Normal difficulty and above \(or on Easy if War Declarations are enabled in the 9973 t-file\), factions may declare war on the player.

Unbreakable Alliances and Total Wars are permanent and bound to the galaxy. They may also be triggered through special Favors.

Coalitions are temporary alliances formed by at least two minor factions against a major faction. Members of an Unbreakable Alliance or Coalition share resources.

Permanent Wars apply only from the player's side. The player may declare a Permanent War against any non-coalition ally at any time. Doing so grants 1 additional perk slot to all current and future Outposts. In addition, every faction engaged in a Total War against the target grant 1 Favor Point toward the player. A Permanent War may also be tied to an existing Total War.

When a faction considers declaring war on the player, it evaluates multiple factors: its current situation, your reputation, loyalty points, infamy, supply consumption, fleet power, and whether you control any of its dejure sectors. Starting as the same faction and maintaining high reputation reduce war likelihood. Higher difficulties, controlling dejure sectors, having infamy, low fleet power, and exceeding your supply limit increase war likelihood.

Instead of declaring war immediately, a faction may issue an Ultimatum demanding one of your sectors. You must own at least two sectors to receive an Ultimatum; otherwise, war is declared outright.

If your reputation is Rank 10 and you own at least two sectors, an Ultimatum is guaranteed. Otherwise, higher reputation and loyalty increase the chance of receiving an Ultimatum instead of a war declaration.

You have 1 hour to comply with an Ultimatum. If you fail to comply - either by missing the deadline or by abandoning or transferring the sector - war is declared. However, if your reputation is Rank 10 at the time of failure, war is averted and your reputation is drastically reduced instead.

Invasions between other factions follow some strict rules:

- A faction cannot claim an already claimed sector.

- Claims have a duration, at the end of which the invader will generally retreat. There is also a cooldown before a Battle Group can claim another sector.

- Battle Groups are always the ones that initiate an invasion. However, they can be reinforced by other fleets, such as Task Forces or Border Patrols.

- A sector is conquered by the claimer when all stations are destroyed. Company stations and Pirate bases are ignored.

- You, as player, automatically claim a sector when you destroy a station.

- Any faction can be completely annihilated.

To defend their territories, invade new sectors and harass the enemy, the main factions have several fleets of different types:

Battle Group: they are used to invade new sectors. They generally tend to regroup to a safe location before claiming the sector they want to conquer, then move towards it.

Border Patrol: they are used to defend border sectors, giving priority to "hot sectors" \(see below\).

Escort: they often escort civilian ships \(Workers\), otherwise they defend their current sector.

Police: they chase ships that have illegal wares onboard and they also attack hostile ships that are in adjacent sectors. By default, they defend their current sector.

Rearguard: they work the exact same way as Border Patrols, except that they focus on non-border sectors.

Task Force: they're the most aggressive fleet. They can go in enemy territory to attack random ships even if they're not in war against them. However, their priority is to destroy enemy satellites and Jump Beacons, as well as assisting Battle Groups. They also have a reprisal mechanics: they will avenge fallen ships by trying to destroy the same value of enemy ships.

Raider: composed of roughly a dozen M3/M4-class fast fighters, this type of fleet will perform guerrilla style war-time deep anti-logistics operations against other hostile factions. This fleet will penetrate enemy space during war time and kill TS-class transports if it gets the opportunity. If they are attacking your empire, they will additionally target your TP-class transports. On harder difficulties, these fleets have an increased chance to raid your empire rather than other factions.

Apart from the reprisal system, there is also the Alert system. Each time a ship is attacked or something dangerous happens, an Alert is risen and the sector becomes "hot" for a short duration. Such sectors will always receive a special attention from most fleets.

Most fleets will retreat when they feel overwhelmed. If that happens, they will go to the nearest safe Outpost and wait for reinforcements.

Missiles have been completely overhauled to reduce confusion between missile types and create a more believable combat model.

There are four missile categories:

- Fox 1: Semi active radar homing missiles. These missiles require a locked target before firing. They are relatively slow and have medium range. Only CCDS MK1 can identify Fox 1 missiles. Identification can be performed at long range and is required before chaffs can be deployed.
- Fox 2: Infrared missiles. These heat-seeking missiles do not require a target lock and can even track other missiles. They are fast and short-ranged, but they are less effective against ships with small heat signatures such as fighters. Only CCDS MK2 can identify Fox 2 missiles, and only at medium range.
- Fox 3: Active radar homing missiles. These missiles do not require a target lock and combine high speed with long range. Only CCDS MK3 can identify Fox 3 missiles, and only at short range.
- Artillery missiles: Passive radar homing missiles designed for specialized missile platforms. They have the highest speed, range, damage, and price of all missile types. Due to their unstable nature, artillery missiles cannot be intercepted with CCDS and chaffs. Like all other missiles however, they can still be destroyed by laser fire, although missiles are far more durable than in vanilla.

Every faction possesses missiles for the Fox categories, while artillery missiles are limited to specialized factions and ships.

The AI has been improved to use missiles efficiently while maintaining performance and balance. NPC ships do not use missiles when out of sector \(your ships still can\) and will generally avoid firing missiles at small fighters. The AI is also capable of using M8 bombers and M7M missile frigates. These ships can always launch missiles during Out-Of-Sector combat, just like player-owned ships. Each M8 also has built-in CCDS with extended missile detection range, allowing it to protect nearby allies from incoming missiles.

Fighters cannot fire missiles. Only M1, M2, M6, M7, M7M, and M8 are capable of using them. Artillery missiles are normally exclusive to M7M frigates, although certain specialized ships may also use them. All other missile classes can fire Fox missiles.

There is no hotkey to manually deploy chaffs. CCDS already have an extremely low failure rate, and no pilot can react faster than a targeting computer.

Hacking allows you to disrupt, damage, or capture ships. To start hacking, you need three things:

- A Hacking Rootkit. This equipment gives you access to the Hacking commands, from your ship console. Those commands are only available to your own ship, ie. the ship you are piloting yourself.
- Hackerchips. Those chips are required to install and uninstall a backdoor on a vulnerable target. You can produce them either at an Outpost, via the Outpost's Cyberwar Center perk, or at a Mobile Factory, the latter being an ST-cargo ship equipped with a Mobile Factory Kit \(craftable from the Hangar -> Upgrade Ships menu of your Outposts\).
- A Hacking station. It's possible to transform your Research station by buying a specific perk at your local Outpost. The Hacking station is used to research vulnerabilities and create new viruses.

Once you get all the requirements, you need to understand how hacking works. Firstly, you need to scan a target \(Hacking -> Scan Target Ports\) or have an Outpost with Cyberwar Center open up ports. That will give you some information about its vulnerable ports \(Hacking -> Show Database Entry\). Those ports are used to access various systems of the target:

- Accounting: steals money from the target's bank account. If you joined the OCV, the hack causes the target to drop a crate of Red Crystals instead.
- Cargo: forces the target to drop part of its cargo.
- Hull Cooling: damages the hull of the target.
- Navigation: temporarily disrupts the controls of the target, forcing it to move randomly to adjacent sectors.
- Oxygen: Kills all crew, allowing the ship to be captured.
- Shields: causes a temporary power outage in the target's systems, affecting both its laser and shield generators.
- Weapons: temporarily disables the ship's weapon systems.

Secondly, you need to install a backdoor on one of the open ports of the targets.

- Closed ports are not vulnerable and cannot be hacked.
- Secured ports can be opened if you spend research on them.
- Open ports can be used to install a backdoor \(at the cost of a Hackerchip\).

Spending research on a port costs money and time. Unlike Research stations, you need to inject funds into the Hacking station to start any research project.

When a ship is equipped with an Advanced Firewall Software, all its ports are closed and it cannot be hacked.

Installing a backdoor is safe, but its vulnerability can be detected. In that case, the port will be shown as "patched" and it will no longer be possible to hack it.

Once you have installed a backdoor on a target, this target becomes vulnerable. You now have access to its systems, and that gives you the ability to inject a virus. Viruses affect only one system, on one vector, but you can affect multiple targets at once. If you need to target the same system on a different vector, you will need to create another virus.

When you create a new virus, you have the choice of choosing efficiency over security and vice versa. It has several effects, especially the maximum range from the Hacking station at which you will be able to dispatch your virus. Targets outside of this range cannot be hacked.

When your virus is ready, you can dispatch it to targets in range. It works as follow:

1/ Select one or several targets. Your virus will affect these targets, on the system the virus has been designed for.
2/ Select relays. A relay is a reachable ship on which you have installed a backdoor. It serves as a proxy that will protect you from being backtraced.
3/ Confirm and dispatch the virus. It will take a while for it to infect the system and have a direct effect. You will be notified.

Targets have a different amount of nodes depending on their size. The more nodes a target has, the longer it will take for the virus to infect a system. Each node is also another chance of being backtraced. If any backtrace succeeded, a counterattack will be launched against several of your ships. This counterattack can affect your own ships the same way you affect your targets. The chance of being backtraced is calculated per each relay, ie. the backtrace has to go through all your relays before reaching your Hacking station and identify you as the hacker. Because cyber attacks are always hard to prove, there will be no other consequences to your attacks \(although counterattacks can be pretty disastrous!\).

Quickhacking is an alternative approach. No Outpost perks are required - all that are needed is a ship with a Hacking Rootkit and 1 Hackerchip. It has a random hack efficiency between 30 to 70% and no delays. However, it does not work on Oxygen or Accounting subsystems and always gets traced back to you. The subsystem is then patched immediately for the entire ship line and all other ports on the quickhacked ship are closed.

In Mayhem 3, all combat scripts have been rewritten from scratch. That means that some basic things have been redesigned. In that regard, combat tactics and ship formations have been overhauled. All formations, squadrons and fleets now have the same rules:

1. The leader is at the center of the formation and only the leader runs the main script that tells him what to do in what situations.

2. Followers are all the other ships that follow the leader and assist him. They will always try to protect the leader in priority, then attack his target, or assist other followers.

3. Support ships are fighters that can be carried by a follower. As soon as they are in the carrier, and while the carrier is alive, they become independent from the formation. Their priority then becomes the protection and the assistance of the carrier. If the carrier dies, they will join the formation back, as standard followers. If the carrier is equipped with a Carrier Repair Module, the support ships will wait there while their hull is damaged.

Note that wings are one of the few things - with turret scripts - that have been left untouched. Please report any problem you might encounter with them.

Loot, aka FLC for Fight Loot Chance is a Litcube's Universe feature that determines how much chance a ship has to drop shields and lasers if he's destroyed by a player's ship. However, in Mayhem, the FLC is a fixed rate that applies to every ship in the universe, including yours. The FLC level that you can see in the Pilot Status screen can be ignored. Freighters are special regarding loot. If they have cargo, they will always drop all their cargo.\n\nBailing rates in Mayhem have been decreased a lot. Abandoned ships are now limited in number, and Mayhem has its own bailing system.

Several hotkeys are crucial to the gameplay of Mayhem. The Personal console is by far the menu you will use the most. You can access it through a hotkey or through the Additional ship commands menu of your ships. Note that all custom hotkeys are deactivated when you are docked \(hardcoded limitation\).

Many gameplay variables can be changed via two simple files: X3/addon/t/9972-L044.xml and X3/addon/t/9973-L044.xml. Almost everything can be adjusted to your taste! These files are often referenced as "t-files".

All ships are repaired over time for free when they are docked at any of your Outposts. They can also be repaired in a carrier if it's equipped with a Carrier Repair Module. However, the process is slower than in an Outpost.

Additionally, a carrier can repair spaceborne ships. However, there are four conditions:
- The follower must not be docked.
- The follower must be part of the fleet.
- Both the carrier and the follower must not be attacking.
- The follower must be a big ship or larger. M6, TM, M8, and any capital ship count.

Stations automatically repair themselves over time.

Lots of equipment are now included by default into all ships. However, for some of them like the Docking Computer and the Transporter Device, you will need to go through the Update ship menu from your Outpost's Hangar and spend some colored crystals to acquire them. These crystals come from mining, but they can also be transmuted from "normal" Crystals, i.e. those produced in Crystal Fabs.\n\nPlease consult the Ship Equipment section of the encyclopedia to learn more about all the new equipment.

Pirates have always been hiding in the darkest corners of the universe, even before the failed terraforming attempts of the Terrans. Pirate bases can be randomly found in unknown sectors. They will create fighters, corvettes, and military transports that will hunt down freighters and their precious cargo.\n\nPirate bases respawn over time, but they will no longer respawn if there are no Pirate bases or Yaki Outposts left in the galaxy. You can dock to any Pirate base at anytime, even if they appear hostile, unless you have destroyed a Pirate base recently. If you want to fix a bad reputation with a faction, you should dock to one of them.
E\) Jump Points - Jump Beacons and Jump Stations

Jump Points refer to your Jump Beacons and Jump Stations. Together, they form your personal gate network across the galaxy.

You are the only faction capable of crafting and deploying Jump Beacons. However, Phanon can use your Jump Points for travel. If you join the OCV, Phanon may also rebuild and operate their own Jump Beacon network.


Jump Beacons

To construct a Jump Beacon:
1. Build a Jumpdrive Core Factory at one of your Outposts.
2. Deploy that factory and have it produce Jumpdrive Cores.
3. Manufacture a Jump Beacon:
 - At an Outpost, or
 - From a ship equipped with a Mobile Factory Kit \(Special -> Manufacture command\)

Jump Beacons function like gates. When at least two are active, your ships will automatically route through them and always seek the shortest available path. You can travel through your Jump Beacons manually using the custom hotkey.


Jump Stations

Outposts can unlock the Jump Station perk. Jump Stations function identically to Jump Beacons, but they are not vulnerable like Beacons.


Jump Point Limits

There is a galaxy-wide limit on the number of active Jump Points. This limit depends on how large your galaxy is. Insane difficulty reduces this limit.


Beacon Security

Jump Beacons are vulnerable to hostile interference.

Xenon forces may infect a Jump Beacon. Once converted, the Beacon becomes a Xenon-controlled spawn point. Infection is irreversible. If you have joined the OCV, your ships will not oppose the conversion.

NPC factions may destroy enemy Jump Beacons in their territory. Pirates may target Beacons regardless of ownership; however, if you have joined the OCV, pirates will instead target only player-owned and Xenon Jump Beacons.

Jump Stations are immune to infection and cannot be destroyed in this manner.


Placement and Maintenance

The following placement and maintenance restrictions apply only on hard and insane difficulties:

To capture, place, or maintain a Jump Beacon, one of the following must be true:
- You own the sector.
- You are a close ally with the sector's faction.
 - Being a close ally requires reputation rank 6 \(7 on insane\) or higher.
- The sector is unknown.
 - If the sector is the Renegades sector, then the Renegades plot must be completed.

You cannot place or capture Jump Beacons in enemy sectors or in faction sectors where your reputation is insufficient.


Abandoned Jump Beacons

Abandoned Jump Beacons can be found in Terran memory sectors. Higher difficulty levels reduce the number of abandoned beacons.

Xenons are the unfortunate consequence of the many failed terraforming attempts lead by the Terrans a few decades ago. They have some heavily defended sectors, and they can spawn invasion fleets. However, the defenders are generic and will not be reinforced over time. Once they're destroyed, the defenders are not rebuilt.

Xenon invaders will try to capture your Jump Beacons in priority after spawning from their stations. They can use those the same way you can.

There is a storyline that lets you ally with the Xenon or work with Phanon, a defective branch of terraformers. While allying with the Xenon comes with great benefits, this comes with its set of challenges.

You can choose the difficulty setting of your game only when you answer the initial survey. This setting affects:

- The strength of Xenon and OCV invasions, wandering Xenon fleets, and Renegade ships.
- The number of Xenon stations per sector \(hence the strength of defensive forces\). 
- The number of pirates that are spawned from Pirate bases.
- The chance of spawning a Pirate base in an Unknown sector.

Higher difficulties add more modifiers, including but not limited to player limitations and more intelligent NPC behavior. These include but are not limited to:

- The general difficulty level of missions.
- Fewer free sectors after conquering your first sector.
- The maximum number of perks you can pick in each Outpost.
- NPC Outposts using additional perks.
- Higher war declaration chance.
- Fewer lasers and shields retained by bailed ships.
- Shorter black market ship timers.
- Reduced tax income.

See the Insane Difficulty section for the full list of modifiers.

Private companies not only have Traders but also mercenaries. During their normal routine, these mercenaries will roam the galaxy, trying to be helpful where they can. Sometimes they will try to smuggle some illegal wares from a faction to another. If you happen to find one, and if you have a Police license, they will turn Pirate and you will be able to gain a bounty by killing them.

Mercenaries can also be hired for your own benefit. If you decide to hire one, you will have to pay a regular fee and assign them to one of your assets, to protect or to escort. They can be dismissed at any time, but doing so below one hour is not optimal, as you need to pay a first single hiring fee that represents an hour of work. Some mercenaries may already have a client; you can hire these mercenaries, but you must pay more to convince them to break their contract with their previous client.

Nomad mercenaries are spawned from the Nomad flagship. These mercenaries are cheaper to hire, but they will eventually leave you. Having infamy gained from piracy such as destroying company traders or boarding will greatly reduce the likelihood that leave you.
From time to time, Kha'ak ships come from deep space to invade the empire that owns the most sectors in the galaxy.

In addition to your ability to conquer sectors by dropping a station in them, you can also buy a sector from the faction you pledged alliance to \(i.e. your specific gamestart\). To buy a sector, you need money and you need to have completed a few missions in that sector. Factions are not willing to sell all their sectors. Instead, they will sell only their cheapest ones and also the ones that are under your influence, i.e. the ones that are adjacent to your sectors. Dejure sectors are never to be sold. Weak empires do not sell any of their sectors.\n\nWhen you buy a sector, you get all the stations, including the Outpost, if any. The more sectors you buy, the more expensive they get.

Terraforming is unlocked when you progress through the storyline, either by helping Phanon or by joining the Xenon/OCV. Terraforming allows you to gain a bonus per planet in your sector. Each time you successfully terraform a planet, its sector will improve its population, research, and station support stats. Effects come in one of three rarities: common, [cyan]uncommon[/cyan], and [magenta]rare[/magenta].

However, it is not without cost. Terraforming projects strain both your sector's and your empire's economy. Terraforming progress is based on how many people are in your sector's Outpost and how many are in that sector's adjacent Outposts. 

By default, you may terraform 1 project at a time in a sector. This local limit can be increased by buying perks. The Terraforming Specialist perk doubles your Outpost's terraforming manpower and increases the limit to 3 projects in that sector.

There are several Outpost perks which can be bought upon terraforming a number of planets. Terraforming efficiency 1 requires only 3 terraformed planets. To unlock the next tier, you must have bought the previous tier and have terraformed the required number of planets. The following Outpost perks are purchasable once you've terraformed a certain number of planets:

- Terraforming Efficiency 1 \(3 planets required\): 1.2x terraforming manpower. 2x manpower instead if you allied with the Xenon.
- Terraforming Efficiency 2 \(7 planets required\): Reduces the global terraforming penalty applied to this Outpost by 33%.
- Terraforming Efficiency 3 \(12 planets required\): Outpost contributes 100% of its population to adjacent terraforming projects instead of 50%.
- Terraforming Efficiency 4 \(18 planets required\): Requires Capital Shipyard upgrade purchased and all other terraforming perks. Gain 10% base max specialization.

By default, your global limit is 1 project. For every 4 \(6 on insane difficulty\) planets within your empire, you may terraform one additional planet. Upon successfully terraforming your 18th planet, you'll have mastered Terraforming. Mastering terraforming reduces the divisor by 1 \(from 4 -> 3, or 6 -> 5 on insane difficulty\) allowing 1 additional terraforming project per 3 planets \(5 on insane difficulty\) instead.

Even though terraforming multiple planets at once divides the manpower equally among all active local projects, it is faster to terraform more than one planet at once than to terraform one planet at a time.

In the Ministry of War, you will notice a specific type of diplomatic actions that is called Favor.

Favor points are bought with Loyalty and allows you to force a faction to act in a certain way. Alternatively, favor points can be acquired by destroying a high-priority target \(M7-class ships with a *\), by destroying a Hive Queen spawned from Kha'ak raids, by joining a Coalition, or by giving a sector to another faction as long as the sector transfer is not because of an ultimatum. These actions can be quite powerful and it's an easy way of influencing the galaxy and making your game your own sandbox.

Loyalty is a currency that is granted every time you finish a mission. Sometimes, destroying a big \(M6, TM, M8\) or a capital ship will award you loyalty with that victim's enemies. Loyalty is used to buy Favors, except if you have activated the "Ship Purchase" feature, from the 9972 t-file, which is deactivated by default. If you are playing on normal difficulty or higher \(or on easy difficulty with war declarations enabled in the 9973 t-file\), then loyalty points increase the chance of getting an ultimatum instead of an outright war declaration.

Aborting a mission will result in losing one loyalty point. Falling below rank 0 or going to war with a faction will result in losing all your loyalty and favor points.

Sectors, stations, wares and entire factions can be blacklisted through a dedicated menu in your Personal console. Those items will then be ignored by most of your ships. It's important to know that all your ships always move through a safe path in the galaxy. That means that they will avoid Xenon sectors, for instance. However, you can decide whether or not they can still be allowed to pass through blacklisted sectors when they need it. By default, blacklisted sectors are considered enemies and as such, your ships will avoid them as much as they can \(sometimes it's just impossible\).

In Mayhem, lasers do not consume energy. The main reason is that during Out-Of-Sector combat, the simulation ignores laser energy, giving infinite energy to all ships. Combat between OOS and In-Sector combat was therefore very imbalanced.

Renegades are an unknown faction that specializes in fast hit-and-run raids against your empire. No one knows who hired them, but their objective is clear: harass your logistics, weaken your defenses, and force you to respond on their terms.

There are three types of Renegade ships: roamers, assassins, and defenders.


Roamers

Roamers are the first Renegade ships you will encounter. Early on, they patrol distant sectors, targeting your satellites and vulnerable ships. If they succeed, they may accelerate to escape and flee toward a station. As your campaign progresses - either because too many roamers are active in the galaxy or because your fleet power is high enough - new roamers will shift from patrol behavior to direct raids against your sectors.

Destroying a roamer yields clues and a crate containing random crystals. The first roamer you destroy begins Renegades plot and reveals the sector containing the hidden gate. After that, additional roamer kills can drop gate code fragments required to unlock the gate to their home sector. Pirate ships have a small chance to provide hints about the Renegades, but they will never drop gate code fragments.

Once you have collected all three gate code fragments, travel to the sector mentioned in the first clue and scan the special shipwreck. The gate code fragments are displayed with dashes for readability. Enter the code and solve the puzzle.

Success opens the gate to the Renegade home sector. Failure triggers immediate retaliation and puts you in grave danger.


Assassins

Assassins appear if you fail the puzzle. They spawn near you and aggressively engage nearby assets. If they achieve their objective, they escalate into raids against your sectors.


Defenders

Defenders reside in the Renegade home sector and serve two purposes:

1. Territorial defense: they protect the Renegade station and surrounding space.

2. Invasion pressure: if you unlock the gate without establishing clear fleet superiority in their home sector, the Renegades may launch an invasion using their defenders as the strike force.


Scaling and Difficulty

Renegade spawns and ship composition scale with game difficulty and your fleet power. Higher difficulties and excessive fleet power lead to more Renegade activity and tougher ship classes.

Destroying the Renegade station in their home sector completes the Renegades plot and awards generous rewards.

Insane difficulty adds additional constraints and scaling on top of Hard:

1. Starting Conditions
- Once you conquer your first sector, all unknown sectors are immediately conquered by other factions, limiting further expansion opportunities.
- Nation status is granted after acquiring a sector or completing 1/3 of one of the required milestones.
- Ascension
 - Quickstart disabled. 
 - Replaced with a special ascension featuring higher quotas and randomized tasks.
- No starting ships, credits, revealed sectors, and blueprints.
- No starting reputation bonus with your origin faction. -1000 reputation with all other Commonwealth factions.
- The Maelstrom \(OCV portal\) is placed in a random Xenon sector, and its location is not revealed at the start.
- In Chaotic galaxies, the galaxy map is no longer fully revealed at the start and must be explored.

2. Player Limitations
- Reduced tutorial guidance.

- Economy and Progression:
 - Maintenance costs increased by 50%.
 - Tax income reduced by 50%.
 - Boarding and Trade Union rewards reduced by 33%.
 - Recycle efficiency reduced by 20%.
 - Renegade roamers drop 33% fewer crystals.
 - Reduced chance of missions that reward ships.

- Logistics and Access:
 - TS and TP restrictions:
 - Black market prices increased by 10x.
 - No TS and TP research or blueprints \(except from main plot rewards\).
 - Capital Shipyard:
 - More expensive.
 - Required to build M7, M2, and M1.

- Intel and Control:
 - Police license, placing or capturing Jump Beacons, and maintaining deployables \(Jump Beacons and satellites\) in NPC sectors require at least Rank 7 reputation.
 - Satellite cleanup is always enabled.
 - Infamy benefits are reduced.

- Systems and Mobility:
 - Terraforming penalties increased; global project limit reduced.
 - Teleportation requires a Transporter Device on the target ship.
 - Jump Beacon and Jump Station caps reduced by 25%.
 - Favor and OCV conversion timer durations reduced by 30%.

3. NPC Behavior

- Combat and Equipment:
 - Reduced ship bail chance. Bailed ships retain even fewer lasers and shields.
 - NPC capital ships are more likely to spawn with Advanced Firewall Software and Internal Sentry Lasers.
 - All TS and TP have a 50% chance to spawn with Advanced Firewall Software.

- Scaling and Aggression:
 - NPC factions are more aggressive, better equipped, and scale their fleet strength more aggressively in response to the player.
 - NPC factions:
 - Less likely to issue ultimatums.
 - Can declare war without a shared border.
 - Raider fleets are more likely to target the player.

- Expansion and Systems:
 - Explorers have a 1% chance to conquer unknown sectors \(vs 0.2% on Hard\).
 - Xenon infect Jump Beacons faster.
 - NPC Outposts and Renegade ships \(does not include Renegade support fighters\) have an increased chance of spawning with Pandora Tuning.
 - Outposts with Pandora Tuning guarantee that all ships they produce inherit Pandora Tuning.

4. Main Plot

- Phanon Playthrough:
 - When allied, Phanon operates at reduced efficiency:
 - 70% production speed. 
 - 63% with player infamy.
 - This penalty is removed after joining the OCV.

- OCV Playthrough:
 - Phanon is more likely to deploy Jump Beacons in both their sectors and Commonwealth sectors.
 - Upon joining:
 - Only one blueprint per ship class.
 - Starting fleet is weaker.
 - Xenon and OCV fleet strength reduced by 50% after joining.
